html:
The bark of the cinchona tree, from the forests of the eastern Andes in Peru, Ecuador and Bolivia, was the first effective medicine against malaria. Europeans learned of it around the 1630s, likely from Quechua healers who used it against fevers and chills.

Jesuit priests in Peru sent it to Rome, and it became known as "Jesuit's bark". Doctors there used it on the fevers that haunted the city's marshes. Some Protestants at first distrusted a "popish" remedy, but by the late 1600s it was widely used in Europe.

In 1820 the French chemists Pelletier and Caventou extracted its active substance, quinine. Quinine let European soldiers and officials survive in malarial lands, which made it a quiet tool of empire, especially in Africa. The Andean countries tried to keep the trees to themselves, but British and Dutch agents smuggled out seeds in the 1850s and 1860s, and plantations in Java came to supply most of the world. Quinine was also the bitter in tonic water.
